criteria.description: Correctly describes the central-difference formula and that it estimates the derivative independently of the analytical formula.
Correctly interprets a single-entry mismatch as pointing to a localized bug (e.g. one term/sign) rather than a wholesale misunderstanding.

commonErrors: Only stating 'it checks if your gradient is right' without explaining the actual mechanism (comparing to an independent finite-difference estimate).
Claiming a single-entry mismatch means the whole derivation is wrong, rather than localizing the likely bug.

solutions.fullSolution: A finite-difference check estimates partial f/partial x_i as [f(x+eps*e_i) - f(x-eps*e_i)] / (2 eps) for small eps, using only evaluations of f itself, never touching your analytical gradient formula. If this numerical estimate matches your analytical gradient closely (for a well-chosen eps, not too big or too small due to floating-point error), your derivation is very likely correct. If only one entry disagrees while the rest match, that's strong evidence of a localized bug affecting just that variable or term (e.g. a dropped factor, sign error, or wrong index) rather than a fundamental error in your whole approach, since a fundamental error would typically show up in most or all entries.

criteria.description: Correctly differentiates the double sum w.r.t. x_k, splitting into the i=k and j=k contributions.
Correctly identifies the first sum as [Ax]_k.
Correctly identifies the second sum as [A^T x]_k, using A_ik = (A^T)_ki.

commonErrors: Assuming A is symmetric and skipping straight to 2Ax (only valid when A=A^T; the general derivation must keep A and A^T separate).
Double-counting or missing the i=j=k diagonal term when splitting the sum.

solutions.fullSolution:
f(x) = sum_{i,j} A_ij x_i x_j. Differentiate w.r.t. x_k using the product rule on each term: a term A_ij x_i x_j contributes A_kj x_j (from x_i=x_k, when i=k) plus A_ik x_i (from x_j=x_k, when j=k); summing over all i,j:
partial f/partial x_k = sum_j A_kj x_j + sum_i A_ik x_i.
The first sum is exactly [Ax]_k (row k of A dotted with x). The second sum, sum_i A_ik x_i, is [A^T x]_k, since (A^T)_ki = A_ik. So partial f/partial x_k = [Ax]_k + [A^T x]_k = [(A+A^T)x]_k for every k, i.e. grad f(x) = (A+A^T)x.
